Agnès Varda. The Belgian-French director and pioneer of cinema-vérité who brought radical subjectivity and poetic observation to both fiction and non-fiction. Her films explore female consciousness, memory, and the texture of everyday life with a visual sensibility influenced by painting and photography, making her a singular voice within and adjacent to the French New Wave.

She directed Cléo from 5 to 7 in 1962, following a woman through ninety minutes of Paris as she awaits a cancer diagnosis. It is a real-time exploration of fear, beauty, and female interiority. Later she made Vagabond in 1985, which won the Palme d'Or. The film backtracks through the life of a young woman found frozen in a ditch, interviewing those she encountered.

Varda pioneered cinema-vérité direct cinema using lightweight cameras and minimal crews, giving her documentary work an immediacy and authenticity. She blended documentary and fiction throughout her career. The Gleaners and I from 2000 intermixes philosophy, portraiture, and personal reflection, challenging genre boundaries. Known for her visual sophistication—colours, compositions, the formal beauty of the image—even in realist contexts, she remained a politically engaged filmmaker whose work often features working-class characters, women, and those society marginalises. She continued making films into her nineties, maintaining formal invention and intellectual vitality.

Her work shares concerns with Jean-Luc Godard, her fellow New Wave figure, though where both questioned narrative and authorship, Varda emphasised collective and personal memory. She shared with Robert Bresson an ascetic sensibility and interest in non-professional acting. She was a contemporary of Alain Resnais, another explorer of memory and subjective time. Her films centre female perspective and experience, making her a foundational figure in feminism in film.
